screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore two complementary features you will use when building resilient, high-throughput campus and data center fabrics. First, link aggregation groups allow you to combine several physical Ethernet links into one logical interface so bandwidth and resilience scale together. You will learn why LAGs matter when a single cable becomes a bottleneck, how LACP negotiates bundles safely, and how to configure and verify an aggregated Ethernet interface on Junos. screens.title: What is a Link Aggregation Group (LAG)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Link Aggregation Group, or LAG, is the practice of combining multiple physical Ethernet links into a single logical interface so that the network treats them as one. The two immediate benefits are higher aggregate bandwidth and link-level redundancy: when links are bundled, traffic can be distributed across them, and the failure of a single physical cable does not bring down the logical connection. In practice, LAGs use a hashing algorithm based on MAC, IP, or transport ports so that individual flows remain on a single physical link while overall utilization rises. A concrete example: two one-gigabit copper links aggregated into ae0 provide up to 2 Gbps of aggregate throughput for multiple flows, while any single flow may still be limited to one physical member depending on hashing. A common misconception is that LAG gives a single TCP stream twice the bandwidth; it usually does not — aggregation improves total capacity across many flows. The takeaway is to use LAGs when you need increased aggregate capacity and graceful failure handling, and plan load-balancing expectations for your traffic mix. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and a practical example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is a LAG?
Definition
A LAG bundles multiple physical Ethernet links into a single logical link for bandwidth aggregation and redundancy.
How it helps
  • Aggregate capacity across links to increase throughput for many flows.
  • Provide link redundancy so service continues if a member fails.
  • Allow a single logical interface to carry VLANs and L2/L3 config.
Concrete example
Two 1 Gbps links form ae0. Multiple clients send traffic using different flows; the bundle supports up to 2 Gbps aggregate traffic. A single flow typically remains on one member due to hashing.
Common mistake
Expecting a single TCP session to automatically use the full aggregated bandwidth — most hashing schemes keep a single flow on one physical link.
Key Takeaway

Use LAGs to increase aggregate throughput and provide link redundancy, but design hashing expectations for your traffic.

Visual: Logical to Physical
Logical: ae0 (single interface)
Physical: ge-0/0/0, ge-0/0/1
Uses: trunk for VLANs
Failure: traffic shifts to remaining members

screens.title: Bandwidth vs. Redundancy — Two benefits of LAG
screens.narratorSegment: When deciding to deploy a LAG you should weigh two primary benefits: increased aggregate bandwidth and link redundancy. Aggregate bandwidth means the bundle presents more total capacity than any single member, which is valuable when many concurrent flows need more throughput. For example, multiple clients communicating across a server farm can collectively use the combined capacity of two or more links. Redundancy is the second benefit: if one physical cable or port fails, the logical ae interface remains up as long as minimum-links is satisfied and the remaining members forward traffic. But these benefits come with trade-offs. Load distribution depends on the hashing algorithm, so single-stream performance may not increase. Also, misconfigured LACP modes or inconsistent VLAN trunking on members can reduce the bundle to a single active link or prevent formation entirely. A practical rule: set minimum-links to a sensible value like one to avoid complete shutdowns, ensure consistent VLANs across members, and use LACP active on at least one side to allow negotiation. Ask yourself: does my traffic pattern need more aggregate throughput or faster per-flow throughput? In practical terms, how aggregation balances throughput and resilience for enterprise links. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Bandwidth vs Redundancy
Aggregate Bandwidth (A)
Multiple active links carry many flows. Total capacity increases roughly proportional to the number of links, improving aggregate throughput for concurrent sessions.
Example: two 1 Gbps links provide up to 2 Gbps for multiple flows.
Misconception: a single TCP flow will not necessarily receive twice the bandwidth.
Key Takeaway

Use LAGs to scale aggregate throughput; verify hashing suits your traffic if you need per-flow scaling.

Link Redundancy (B)
If a physical link fails, LACP and the LAG remove that member and traffic continues on remaining active members when minimum-links allows it.
Example: one cable failure leaves ae0 up if minimum-links is 1, preventing downtime.
Common pitfall: mismatched VLANs or LACP modes can prevent failover or cause traffic loss.
Check: set consistent VLAN membership on ae members and confirm LACP state to ensure redundancy behaves as expected.

screens.title: How LACP Negotiation Works
screens.narratorSegment: LACP is the protocol that automates the formation of Link Aggregation Groups and protects against bundling mismatches. At the highest level, LACP exchanges protocol frames between ports to identify compatible peers and form an aggregated bundle. LACP operates in two modes: active and passive. An active port actively sends negotiation frames to establish a bundle, while a passive port only responds to frames it receives. For a dynamic LAG to form, at least one side must be active. The protocol also carries state information so that failed links are detected and removed from the bundle. During negotiation, LACP checks key parameters such as system priority, port priority, and whether the member supports aggregation, and it will only include links with matching operational characteristics. A common troubleshooting step is to verify that both sides have consistent settings for speed, duplex, and VLAN tagging. Misconfigurations such as both sides set to passive will result in no negotiation and a non-formed bundle; the solution is to enable active on one or both ends. Think of LACP as the safety handshake that ensures only healthy, compatible links participate in a LAG.

keyIdea.title: LACP role
keyIdea.text: LACP negotiates bundles, detects failed links, and ensures only compatible ports join the LAG; require at least one active side for formation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › LACP Negotiation
Negotiation steps
  1. Ports exchange LACP frames identifying system and port attributes.
  2. Matching attributes result in bundle membership; incompatible members are excluded.
  3. Active ports initiate negotiation; passive ports reply.
  4. LACP monitors link health and removes failed members automatically.
Troubleshooting tip
If the LAG does not form, check both sides for active/passive settings, speed/duplex mismatches, and VLAN tagging consistency.
Common misconfiguration
Both ends in passive mode will not initiate negotiation, leaving links unbundled. Ensure one or both sides are active to form the LACP bundle.
Check: set interfaces aeX aggregated-ether-options lacp active on at least one side.
Verify: show lacp interfaces and show interfaces aeX to confirm member state.
Reflect: When would you prefer static bundling instead of LACP? Consider link predictability versus automatic recovery.

screens.title: Configuring a LAG on Juniper EX Series
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring a LAG on Juniper EX Series switches is a sequence of clear steps in Junos. First, create the aggregated Ethernet interface and set sensible aggregated-ether-options: minimum-links ensures the logical interface stays up when at least that many members are active, and enabling lacp active allows dynamic negotiation. Next, assign the physical interfaces to the ae interface using ether-options 802.3ad and the ae identifier. Finally, configure Layer 2 or Layer 3 attributes on the ae interface as you would on a physical port, for example setting a trunk mode and adding VLAN membership. A concrete CLI example shows creating ae0 with minimum-links 1 and lacp active, then binding ge-0/0/0 and ge-0/0/1 to ae0, and setting ae0 unit 0 as a switching trunk for VLAN 10. Common mistakes include forgetting minimum-links and therefore bringing the bundle down when a member fails, or mismatching trunk configuration across members. After committing, verify with show interfaces ae0 and show lacp interfaces to confirm member state and aggregated throughput. Configuring a LAG on Juniper EX Series means create aggregated interfaces first, enable lacp and minimum-links, assign member ports, then configure the ae unit for switching or routing and verify state.. In practical terms, step-by-step junos commands to create ae0, enable lacp, and assign member ports. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Configure LAG (Junos)
Starter Junos commands
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options minimum-links 1
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp active
set interfaces ae0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching port-mode trunk
set interfaces ae0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members DATA

set interfaces ge-0/0/0 ether-options 802.3ad ae0
set interfaces ge-0/0/1 ether-options 802.3ad ae0
After committing, use show interfaces ae0 and show lacp interfaces to confirm the bundle status and active members. If VLANs are carried, ensure the ae unit is configured as a trunk and VLAN membership matches the peer configuration.
Pro tip: set minimum-links to the lowest acceptable number to keep service running if member links fail.
Mistake to avoid: mismatching trunk VLANs on member ports which can cause traffic loss or learning issues.
Example scenario
You have two physical links from Switch-3 to the Virtual Chassis. Configure ae0 with LACP active on both sides and assign VLAN 10 as a trunk to carry data across the bundle.
Key Takeaway

Follow the create-enable-assign-verify pattern when building LAGs on Junos.

screens.title: Verifying LAGs and Common Troubleshooting Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is critical after configuring LAGs. On Junos the primary commands are show interfaces aeX to view the aggregated interface and its member state, and show lacp interfaces to see per-port LACP status. When you run these checks, confirm that the ae interface is up, member links show as bundled, and LACP state indicates active negotiation or bundled. Inspect counters for mismatches and check VLAN membership on the ae unit and on the remote peer. Typical problems include both sides configured as passive — this prevents negotiation and leaves links unbundled — mismatched VLANs which cause traffic to be dropped or learning issues, and forgetting minimum-links which can bring the ae interface down if a single member remains active. Another common troubleshooting tip is to check speed and duplex settings on physical members; they should match and be compatible with aggregation. Finally, analyze traffic behavior: if total traffic stays at a single link, re-evaluate the hashing algorithm and whether your traffic consists of many flows or a few large streams. A thoughtful verification routine prevents surprises in production. screens.title: What is a Juniper Virtual Chassis?
screens.narratorSegment: A Juniper Virtual Chassis allows multiple physical EX Series switches to operate together as one logical device under a single control plane. This architecture simplifies configuration and monitoring because you manage member switches as a single entity. Virtual Chassis increases port density by combining physical ports across members, and provides high availability through a redundant control plane with Master and Backup roles. In addition, spanning tree and forwarding run across the logical chassis rather than per physical member, reducing complexity. Typical use-cases include deploying a pair of EX switches as a high-availability aggregation or core pair, or combining multiple access switches to present a single logical edge. Key cautions are required: correct VCP cabling for redundancy, matching compatible hardware or Junos versions, and explicit mastership-priority to ensure predictable elections. A major risk is split-brain if VC cabling or priorities are configured incorrectly. Use Virtual Chassis when you want operational simplicity and high availability across multiple physical switches. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Virtual Chassis increases port density by combining physical ports across members, and provides high availability through a redundant control plane with Master and Backup roles. In addition, spanning tree and forwarding run across the logical chassis rather than per physical member, reducing complexity. Typical use-cases include deploying a pair of EX switches as a high-availability aggregation or core pair, or combining multiple access switches to present a single logical edge. Key cautions are required: correct VCP cabling for redundancy, matching compatible hardware or Junos versions, and explicit mastership-priority to ensure predictable elections. A major risk is split-brain if VC cabling or priorities are configured incorrectly. Use Virtual Chassis when you want operational simplicity and high availability across multiple physical switches. Architecture and benefits
  • Simplified management: one CLI and one configuration for multiple switches.
  • Increased port density: combined ports appear as one logical switch.
  • High availability: Master and Backup roles protect the control plane.
Use-case
Two EX switches as an aggregation pair that presents a single logical core with redundant control and combined uplinks to the distribution layer.
Cautions
Ensure correct VCP cabling topologies for redundancy, avoid mixing incompatible hardware or software images, and assign mastership-priority for predictable role election.
Risk
Incorrect cabling or missing priorities can lead to a split-brain where two switches think they are Master, disrupting forwarding and management.

screens.title: Virtual Chassis Roles and Mastership Election
screens.narratorSegment: In a Virtual Chassis, each member switch assumes a role that determines how it participates in the control plane. The Master is the active control plane that manages configuration, routing, and forwarding decisions. The Backup is a hot standby that takes over if the Master fails. Linecard members forward traffic but do not hold the active control plane. Role election uses multiple factors: an explicit mastership-priority value, the current role, uptime, and other internal criteria. Setting mastership-priority explicitly is best practice to avoid nondeterministic elections during reboots or partial failures. You assign member roles and serial numbers so each physical device maps predictably to a logical ID. In practice, administrators set the intended Master with a high priority (for example, 255), set the Backup to a lower but high priority, and leave other members as default. Misunderstanding elections can lead to surprises during maintenance, so validate the current master with show virtual-chassis and consider scripted checks in operational procedures. The guided question to carry forward is: who should be Master in your deployment, and how will you ensure it remains so after upgrades?

screens.narratorSegment: Forming a Virtual Chassis begins with cabling and port configuration. If your platform requires it, convert specific PIC slots or ports into Virtual Chassis Ports; otherwise use dedicated VCPs. For example, you may convert ge-0/1/0 and ge-0/1/1 into VCPs when dedicated ports are not available. Next, pre-configure virtual-chassis member mappings including serial numbers and desired roles to avoid surprises. Verify formation with show virtual-chassis and show virtual-chassis status which reports member IDs, roles, and VCP link status. A common error is incorrect cabling that prevents a ring or redundant topology — that can result in single points of failure. screens.title: Hands-on Scenario: Two-member VC and a Third Switch via LAG
screens.narratorSegment: In the hands-on activity you will form a two-member Virtual Chassis and connect a third switch via a LAG. Start by planning numbering: assign Switch-1 as member 0 and Switch-2 as member 1, and set mastership-priority 255 on member 0 and 128 on member 1 for predictable roles. Cable Switch-1 and Switch-2 using VCPs or converted ports so they form a redundant ring or direct link. Once the VC forms, log into the Master and create ae0 on the Virtual Chassis, set aggregated-ether-options minimum-links 1 and enable lacp active. On the VC, assign member 0 physical ports ge-0/0/0 and ge-0/0/1 to ae0 and configure ae0 unit 0 as a trunk with VLAN 10. On Switch-3, configure an ae0 LAG with the two ge ports, set lacp active, and configure it as a trunk for VLAN 10. After committing on both sides, verify with show lacp interfaces and show interfaces ae0 to ensure the bundle formed and VLAN 10 flows across the LAG. Finally, simulate a link or member failure to confirm traffic remains available and that the Backup takes over if you power cycle the Master.

screens.title: Common LAG and Virtual Chassis Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes cause most LAG and Virtual Chassis issues. First, configuring both ends of a LACP link in passive mode prevents negotiation; the fix is to set at least one side to active. Second, inconsistent VLAN or trunk configuration across member ports causes dropped frames or MAC-learning confusion; always configure VLAN membership on the ae unit rather than individual member interfaces. Third, not setting minimum-links can cause an ae interface to go down when only one member remains active; pick a sensible minimum to preserve service. For Virtual Chassis, incorrect VCP cabling that does not form a redundant ring can leave the VC vulnerable to single points of failure. Also, failing to set mastership-priority leads to unpredictable Master selection after reboots; explicitly assign priorities for production devices. Finally, mixing incompatible hardware or software images can block VC formation — always consult release notes and test compatibility in a lab. The corrective routine is systematic verification: check LACP state, VLAN mapping, physical link parameters, VCP connectivity, and run controlled failover tests to validate behavior before deploying to production. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore two complementary features you will use when building resilient, high-throughput campus and data center fabrics. First, link aggregation groups allow you to combine several physical Ethernet links into one logical interface so bandwidth and resilience scale together. Second, Juniper’s Virtual Chassis lets multiple EX Series switches present a single control plane, simplifying management and enabling redundant forwarding and control roles. You will learn why LAGs matter when a single cable becomes a bottleneck, how LACP negotiates bundles safely, and how to configure and verify an aggregated Ethernet interface on Junos. Then we will examine Virtual Chassis architecture, how members assume master, backup, or linecard roles, and why setting mastership-priority matters for predictable elections. A practical scenario ties both features together: two switches form a Virtual Chassis, a third joins via an LACP LAG, and you’ll verify traffic and state. By the end, you’ll understand the operational tradeoffs, how to avoid common misconfigurations like mismatched LACP modes or incorrect VCP cabling, and when to use each tool in a production network.

These objectives map to the hands-on and verification tasks you'll complete. First, you will explain how Link Aggregation Groups combine multiple physical links to increase aggregate bandwidth and provide link redundancy. That includes the reasons to use LAGs and an example where two 1 Gbps links yield higher aggregate capacity. Second, you'll describe how LACP works to form dynamic LAGs, including active and passive modes and why at least one side must be active. Third, you will configure and verify LAGs on Juniper EX switches — creating an ae interface, setting minimum-links, enabling LACP, assigning member interfaces, and checking state with relevant show commands. Finally, you will describe and configure Juniper Virtual Chassis: converting ports to VCPs, assigning member IDs and roles, setting mastership-priority for predictable election, and verifying the VC health. Each objective also includes a practical competency milestone so you can demonstrate the skill in a lab or emulator.

This second objectives screen focuses on hands-on skills and avoiding errors. You will learn the precise Junos steps to form a LAG: create an ae interface, set aggregated-ether-options minimum-links so the bundle stays up when one link remains, and enable lacp active for dynamic negotiation. You will practice assigning member interfaces to the bundle and configuring ae0 as a trunk for VLAN traffic. Next, for Virtual Chassis you will convert ports to Virtual Chassis Ports when required, set member IDs and roles tied to serial numbers, and commit the configuration so the VC forms. For verification, you will use show interfaces ae0 and show lacp interfaces to confirm member state, and show virtual-chassis to check member roles. Finally, this objective asks you to recognize and correct common mistakes like both sides in passive LACP, incorrect VCP cabling that breaks redundancy, or forgetting to set mastership-priority which can lead to unpredictable elections.

A Link Aggregation Group, or LAG, is the practice of combining multiple physical Ethernet links into a single logical interface so that the network treats them as one. The two immediate benefits are higher aggregate bandwidth and link-level redundancy: when links are bundled, traffic can be distributed across them, and the failure of a single physical cable does not bring down the logical connection. In practice, LAGs use a hashing algorithm based on MAC, IP, or transport ports so that individual flows remain on a single physical link while overall utilization rises. A concrete example: two one-gigabit copper links aggregated into ae0 provide up to 2 Gbps of aggregate throughput for multiple flows, while any single flow may still be limited to one physical member depending on hashing. A common misconception is that LAG gives a single TCP stream twice the bandwidth; it usually does not — aggregation improves total capacity across many flows. The takeaway is to use LAGs when you need increased aggregate capacity and graceful failure handling, and plan load-balancing expectations for your traffic mix. What is a Link Aggregation Group (LAG)? means lags present multiple links as a single logical interface to increase total throughput and provide resilience if a member link fails.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and a practical example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When deciding to deploy a LAG you should weigh two primary benefits: increased aggregate bandwidth and link redundancy. Aggregate bandwidth means the bundle presents more total capacity than any single member, which is valuable when many concurrent flows need more throughput. For example, multiple clients communicating across a server farm can collectively use the combined capacity of two or more links. Redundancy is the second benefit: if one physical cable or port fails, the logical ae interface remains up as long as minimum-links is satisfied and the remaining members forward traffic. But these benefits come with trade-offs. Load distribution depends on the hashing algorithm, so single-stream performance may not increase. Also, misconfigured LACP modes or inconsistent VLAN trunking on members can reduce the bundle to a single active link or prevent formation entirely. A practical rule: set minimum-links to a sensible value like one to avoid complete shutdowns, ensure consistent VLANs across members, and use LACP active on at least one side to allow negotiation. Ask yourself: does my traffic pattern need more aggregate throughput or faster per-flow throughput? Bandwidth vs. Redundancy — Two benefits of LAG means lags provide both capacity and resilience, but hashing and misconfigurations affect how much per-flow performance improves.. In practical terms, how aggregation balances throughput and resilience for enterprise links. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

LACP is the protocol that automates the formation of Link Aggregation Groups and protects against bundling mismatches. At the highest level, LACP exchanges protocol frames between ports to identify compatible peers and form an aggregated bundle. LACP operates in two modes: active and passive. An active port actively sends negotiation frames to establish a bundle, while a passive port only responds to frames it receives. For a dynamic LAG to form, at least one side must be active. The protocol also carries state information so that failed links are detected and removed from the bundle. During negotiation, LACP checks key parameters such as system priority, port priority, and whether the member supports aggregation, and it will only include links with matching operational characteristics. A common troubleshooting step is to verify that both sides have consistent settings for speed, duplex, and VLAN tagging. Misconfigurations such as both sides set to passive will result in no negotiation and a non-formed bundle; the solution is to enable active on one or both ends. Think of LACP as the safety handshake that ensures only healthy, compatible links participate in a LAG.

Configuring a LAG on Juniper EX Series switches is a sequence of clear steps in Junos. First, create the aggregated Ethernet interface and set sensible aggregated-ether-options: minimum-links ensures the logical interface stays up when at least that many members are active, and enabling lacp active allows dynamic negotiation. Next, assign the physical interfaces to the ae interface using ether-options 802.3ad and the ae identifier. Finally, configure Layer 2 or Layer 3 attributes on the ae interface as you would on a physical port, for example setting a trunk mode and adding VLAN membership. A concrete CLI example shows creating ae0 with minimum-links 1 and lacp active, then binding ge-0/0/0 and ge-0/0/1 to ae0, and setting ae0 unit 0 as a switching trunk for VLAN 10. Common mistakes include forgetting minimum-links and therefore bringing the bundle down when a member fails, or mismatching trunk configuration across members. After committing, verify with show interfaces ae0 and show lacp interfaces to confirm member state and aggregated throughput. Configuring a LAG on Juniper EX Series means create aggregated interfaces first, enable lacp and minimum-links, assign member ports, then configure the ae unit for switching or routing and verify state.. In practical terms, step-by-step junos commands to create ae0, enable lacp, and assign member ports. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Verification is critical after configuring LAGs. On Junos the primary commands are show interfaces aeX to view the aggregated interface and its member state, and show lacp interfaces to see per-port LACP status. When you run these checks, confirm that the ae interface is up, member links show as bundled, and LACP state indicates active negotiation or bundled. Inspect counters for mismatches and check VLAN membership on the ae unit and on the remote peer. Typical problems include both sides configured as passive — this prevents negotiation and leaves links unbundled — mismatched VLANs which cause traffic to be dropped or learning issues, and forgetting minimum-links which can bring the ae interface down if a single member remains active. Another common troubleshooting tip is to check speed and duplex settings on physical members; they should match and be compatible with aggregation. Finally, analyze traffic behavior: if total traffic stays at a single link, re-evaluate the hashing algorithm and whether your traffic consists of many flows or a few large streams. A thoughtful verification routine prevents surprises in production. A Juniper Virtual Chassis allows multiple physical EX Series switches to operate together as one logical device under a single control plane. This architecture simplifies configuration and monitoring because you manage member switches as a single entity. Virtual Chassis increases port density by combining physical ports across members, and provides high availability through a redundant control plane with Master and Backup roles. In addition, spanning tree and forwarding run across the logical chassis rather than per physical member, reducing complexity. Typical use-cases include deploying a pair of EX switches as a high-availability aggregation or core pair, or combining multiple access switches to present a single logical edge. Key cautions are required: correct VCP cabling for redundancy, matching compatible hardware or Junos versions, and explicit mastership-priority to ensure predictable elections. A major risk is split-brain if VC cabling or priorities are configured incorrectly. Use Virtual Chassis when you want operational simplicity and high availability across multiple physical switches. In a Virtual Chassis, each member switch assumes a role that determines how it participates in the control plane. The Master is the active control plane that manages configuration, routing, and forwarding decisions. The Backup is a hot standby that takes over if the Master fails. Linecard members forward traffic but do not hold the active control plane. Role election uses multiple factors: an explicit mastership-priority value, the current role, uptime, and other internal criteria. Setting mastership-priority explicitly is best practice to avoid nondeterministic elections during reboots or partial failures. You assign member roles and serial numbers so each physical device maps predictably to a logical ID. In practice, administrators set the intended Master with a high priority (for example, 255), set the Backup to a lower but high priority, and leave other members as default. Misunderstanding elections can lead to surprises during maintenance, so validate the current master with show virtual-chassis and consider scripted checks in operational procedures. The guided question to carry forward is: who should be Master in your deployment, and how will you ensure it remains so after upgrades?

Assign master and backup roles explicitly and set mastership-priority values to influence election. Several recurring mistakes cause most LAG and Virtual Chassis issues. First, configuring both ends of a LACP link in passive mode prevents negotiation; the fix is to set at least one side to active. Second, inconsistent VLAN or trunk configuration across member ports causes dropped frames or MAC-learning confusion; always configure VLAN membership on the ae unit rather than individual member interfaces. Third, not setting minimum-links can cause an ae interface to go down when only one member remains active; pick a sensible minimum to preserve service. For Virtual Chassis, incorrect VCP cabling that does not form a redundant ring can leave the VC vulnerable to single points of failure. Also, failing to set mastership-priority leads to unpredictable Master selection after reboots; explicitly assign priorities for production devices. Finally, mixing incompatible hardware or software images can block VC formation — always consult release notes and test compatibility in a lab. The corrective routine is systematic verification: check LACP state, VLAN mapping, physical link parameters, VCP connectivity, and run controlled failover tests to validate behavior before deploying to production. Keep these concise concepts in mind as you design and operate networks. A Link Aggregation Group bundles multiple physical links into one logical interface to increase aggregate bandwidth and provide link redundancy. LACP is the standard protocol that dynamically negotiates LAG members and ensures only compatible ports are bundled; remember that at least one side must be active for negotiation. Virtual Chassis makes multiple Juniper EX switches appear as a single logical device with a single control plane, improving manageability and providing redundant Master and Backup roles. Always verify with show interfaces aeX, show lacp interfaces, and show virtual-chassis, and avoid common mistakes such as passive-only LACP, inconsistent VLANs across members, missing minimum-links, improper VCP cabling, or unpredictable master elections without explicit priorities. As a final quick reference, remember these three compact ideas. First, always plan LACP modes and minimum-links: set lacp active on at least one side and choose a minimum-links value that keeps service during member failures. Second, configure ae interfaces on the Virtual Chassis after the VC is formed by the Master, so the logical interface spans the chassis correctly; assign VLANs on the ae unit. Third, predefine mastership-priority and use serial-number-based member assignments to make master election deterministic and avoid split-brain or surprises during maintenance. Keep verification commands in your toolkit and run controlled failover tests in the lab before production rollout.
